title: If a few standard tests find no regularity, other simple programs rarely do

fields.label: Label
fields.value: If a few standard tests find no regularity, other simple programs rarely do

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Once a few simple programs corresponding to standard methods of perception and analysis have failed to detect regularities in some data, it is extremely rare for any other simple program to succeed, so the everyday judgment of randomness is in practice fairly unambiguous.

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. 10: Processes of Perception and Analysis

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: For once a few simple programs corresponding to a few standard methods of perception and analysis have failed to detect regularities, it is extremely rare for any other simple program to succeed in detecting them.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci A New Kind of Science claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Stephen Wolfram, A New Kind of Science (Champaign, IL: Wolfram Media, 2002), Chapter 10, “Processes of Perception and Analysis”; section “Defining the Notion of Randomness” (from p. 552), p. 556. Scope: detection of regularities in sequences and images by simple programs

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on wolfram2002-ch10-05: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.66

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: A broad computational benchmark can directly measure the asserted rarity for specified bounds. It cannot justify the unrestricted quantifier over all simple programs or everyday data.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Sample a preregistered distribution of sequences, images, standard tests, and bounded-description programs, then estimate how often a later program detects held-out regularity after the standard tests fail. A non-negligible rate refutes rarity within that defined universe.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Finite tests cannot quantify all simple programs.

No natural distribution over simple programs.

Detection success depends on sample length and significance threshold.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
discriminating power: 0.65
data adequacy: 0.45
data existence: 0.9

analysis feasibility: 0.65

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Standard test suites and large sequence archives exist, and enumerating very short programs is feasible. That can estimate how often a further short program finds structure after a few standard tests fail, for a bounded class. It cannot cover every simple program, so the claim's unrestricted rarity statement stays only partly tested.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Take sequences and images that pass a fixed set of standard tests, then enumerate simple programs up to a length cutoff and measure how often another program detects a regularity. A high rate of extra detections would refute 'extremely rare'; a near-zero rate inside the cutoff supports the claim only inside that cutoff.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
A regularity can be invisible to every test in a chosen finite set without being absent.

The space of simple programs is unbounded, so 'any other simple program' can be searched only up to a size limit.
